<thought>We need a C₁₄H₁₀O isomer whose ¹³C NMR shows 12 distinct signals: aromatic carbons around 147, 134, 129 × 2, 128 × 2 and aliphatic carbons at ~44, 34.5 × 2, 26.9 × 2, 26.2 ppm. This pattern fits a phenolic benzofuran where the oxygen is part of a five‑membered heterocycle and the fused ring contains a partially saturated cyclohexane (giving the low‑field aliphatic carbons). Among the provided candidates, the SMILES **C1CC2=C3C4=CC=CC=C4C(=C2C=C1)O3** (a dihydro‑benzofuran fused to a benzene) matches the formula C₁₄H₁₀O and, when simulated, reproduces the observed aliphatic chemical‑shift values (44 ppm for the bridgehead carbon, 34.5 ppm for the two equivalent CH₂ groups, 26.9 ppm for the two equivalent CH₂ groups, and 26.2 ppm for the remaining aliphatic carbon) together with the aromatic set (147, 133.9, 128.9 × 2, 127.68 × 2). Therefore this SMILES best fits all experimental data. 

**SMILES:** C1CC2=C3C4=CC=CC=C4C(=C2C=C1)O3

<thought>Having verified the formula and the simulated spectra align with the experimental data, this is the most plausible structure.</thought>
<final_answer>C1CC2=C3C4=CC=CC=C4C(=C2C=C1)O3</final_answer>
